panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial CT demonstrating heterogeneous hepatic enhancement and IVC stenosis in chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome. C: Axial CT showing intrahepatic venous collaterals, narrowed IVC, and nonvisualized hepatic veins indicative of Budd-Chiari syndrome. D: Axial CT demonstrating multiple enhancing hepatic nodules, consistent with regenerative nodules or other sequelae in chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome.

panels.figure_caption: A total of 35 years female presented to the radiology department with chronic abdominal pain. Triphasic computed tomography (CT) abdomen reveals; (A) Chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) manifested as Enlarged liver with heterogeneous enhancement and a patchy hepatogram with areas of hypoperfusion (Red arrows). The hepatic part of inferior vena cava (IVC) shows a focal stenosis which may indicate the presence of an IVC web (Black arrow). (B) The caudate lobe is disproportionately enlarged compared to the rest of the liver. No IVC/portal vein thrombosis. (C) There are multiple intrahepatic collateral vessels, some of which drain directly into the IVC (yellow arrows) and narrow IVC (red arrow) with no enhancement of the hepatic veins (HVs) (inability to identify HVs). (D) There are multiple enhancing nodules spread throughout the liver (Red arrow) as an example.

panels.figure_caption: Perfusion-related pseudo-lesion in a 19-year-old male patient with acute Budd–Chiari syndrome. On the unenhanced (A) and portal venous phase (B) CT images a large mass-like alteration with irregular and ill-defined margins is appreciable in the central region of the right liver lobe (arrows). The thrombosed right hepatic vein (arrowhead) is also visible. On MRI, the fat-saturated T2-weighted imaging (C) demonstrates that the pseudo-lesion consists of normal liver tissue surrounded by congested hyperintense parenchyma (asterisks). On DWI (D), no areas of abnormal restriction are observed as well. Gradient-echo T1 weighted images in the portal (E) and hepatobiliary (F) phases confirm the perfusion-related nature of the pseudo-lesion, showing delayed and decreased enhancement in the congested areas (asterisks).
in_text_mentions: ecially in acute or subacute BCS with proximal venous obstruction [51]. After contrast agent administration, areas of venous congestion may show a peculiar “mosaic pattern” (Figure 9), with patchy and/or peripheral areas of transient enhancement, instead of the classical wedge-shaped alterations [52]. These perfusion anomalies may simulate the presence of lesions, especially considering that the areas of parenchymal congestion appear heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted and hypointense on T1-weighted sequences compared to the caudate, where the drainage is usually preserved (Figure 10).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Coronal contrast-enhanced CT of a patient with Budd-Chiari syndrome demonstrating complete thrombosis (non-filling) of the left and middle hepatic veins, a core diagnostic imaging finding for the disease. B: Axial contrast-enhanced CT of a patient with Budd-Chiari syndrome demonstrating a slit-like compressed intrahepatic inferior vena cava, a classic imaging finding secondary to hepatic venous outflow obstruction. C: Axial contrast-enhanced CT of a patient with Budd-Chiari syndrome demonstrating a heterogeneous mottled (nutmeg) hepatic parenchymal enhancement, a classic finding of hepatic venous congestion in the disease. D: Axial contrast-enhanced CT of a patient with Budd-Chiari syndrome demonstrating caudate lobe hypertrophy, a common compensatory finding in hepatic venous outflow obstruction.

The chest X-ray revealed blunting of the left costophrenic angle, suggestive of a left-sided pleural effusion (Figure 1). The CT scan demonstrated hepatomegaly with diffusely homogeneous liver parenchyma, consistent with acute hepatitis. The caudate lobe was markedly hypertrophic (Figure 2). Additionally, large-volume ascites and thickening of the omental fat were noted. No masses or enlarged lymph nodes were identified.

tion, an abdominal ultrasound with Doppler was performed. This revealed loss of normal respiratory variation in the hepatic and suprahepatic veins, suggestive of hepatic venous outflow obstruction (Figure 3). Subsequent abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed these findings, demonstrating hepatomegaly with a markedly enlarged caudate lobe, absent hepatic veins, and a narrowed portal vein with evidence of intraluminal thrombosis (Figure 2). panels.figure_caption: Contrast-enhanced CT showing findings characteristic of Budd-Chiari syndrome. (A) Non-contrast coronal CT showing hepatomegaly (arrow), caudate lobe hypertrophy (arrowhead), and ascites (asterisk). (B) Coronal portal venous phase with contrast showing hepatomegaly (arrow), caudate lobe hypertrophy (arrowhead), ascites (asterisk), and central-predominant enhancement with peripheral hypoenhancement (curved arrow), consistent with hepatic venous outflow obstruction. (C, D) Axial portal venous phase images showing caudate lobe hypertrophy (arrowhead), ascites (asterisk), and a mottled “nutmeg” liver appearance (curved arrow) reflecting centrilobular congestion. These combined findings - hepatomegaly, ascites, caudate lobe hypertrophy, central enhancement, and “nutmeg” pattern - are characteristic of Budd-Chiari syndrome.
in_text_mentions: A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan revealed hepatomegaly with caudate and left lobe hypertrophy, heterogeneous hepatic parenchymal enhancement, and moderate-to-large ascites. The right hepatic lobe measured approximately 18.7 cm in craniocaudal span (normal: <15 cm), and the caudate lobe measured 4.8 cm in transverse diameter (normal: <3.5 cm), confirming radiologic hepatomegaly. Hepatic veins were not visualized, suggestive of hepatic venous outflow obstruction. Representative imaging findings are shown in Figure 1A-1D.

Abdominal CT scan (Figure 1) and MRI (Figure 2) confirmed thrombosis of the portal vein, suprahepatic vein, and inferior vena cava extending to the right atrium, associated with a hepatic tumor. An ECG was performed to better characterize the intra-auricular thrombus (Figure 3). The diagnosis of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC) was confirmed by liver biopsy. Medical treatment was started immediately with anticoagulation and chemotherapy
